entities.summary:
UBS Group AG is Switzerland's largest bank and one of the world's major wealth management institutions, formed through the 1998 merger of Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS) and Swiss Bank Corporation. As the world's largest private wealth manager with $3.9 trillion in assets under management, UBS serves ultra-high-net-worth individuals, sovereign wealth funds, and institutional investors across 50+ countries.

Switzerland's banking secrecy tradition, codified in the 1934 Federal Banking Act, made Swiss banks the global repository for assets requiring discretion — from Nazi-era Jewish accounts to tax evaders to legitimate wealth. UBS benefited from this tradition before becoming the subject of the most consequential banking secrecy dispute in history: a 2007 US Department of Justice investigation into UBS helping American clients evade taxes through secret accounts. In 2009, UBS agreed to pay $780 million in fines and provide names of 4,450 American account holders — effectively ending Swiss banking secrecy as traditionally practiced.

UBS also suffered a 2008 financial crisis loss of $21 billion from subprime mortgage investments, requiring a 6 billion Swiss franc emergency bailout from the Swiss government. The bank's 2023 emergency acquisition of Credit Suisse — UBS's chief Swiss rival — for 3 billion Swiss francs (compared to Credit Suisse's book value of 45 billion) prevented a banking crisis but created a bank with a $1.6 trillion balance sheet larger than Switzerland's entire GDP, raising 'too big to fail' concerns for a small nation.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: UBS's 2009 surrender of 4,450 client names to the US DOJ effectively ended Swiss banking secrecy — a 75-year tradition that had sheltered wealth from Nazi persecution to tax evasion — transforming global private banking forever.
